title: Beyond rubber: How Pala turned farm crisis into a thriving food processing revolution
content: It is a common misconception across Kerala that agriculture in Pala begins and ends with rubber. For generations, lush homesteads along the Meenachil river thrived with plantains, tapioca, jackfruit, ginger, turmeric, nutmeg, and cloves. However, when rubber prices plummeted, the entire rural farming ecosystem took a hit. Recognising that declining farm incomes threatened both rural livelihoods and nutritional security, the Bishop of Pala diocese, Mar Joseph Kallarangatt, stepped in to drive a structured intervention in the agricultural sector. The initiative began under the leadership of the Pala Social Welfare Society (PSWS), the social service wing of the diocese, by setting up self-reliant farmer groups (Karshakadalams) in every parish. The vision was to build a community-driven institution providing manpower, funding, and innovative ideas to support growers. Over time, 215 self-help groups coalesced into 18 farmers' clubs, which eventually evolved into 7 Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs). Celebrating the diocese's platinum jubilee, the SantHome Food Factory was established as a centralized venture. Its operating arm, SantHome Producer Company, established to bring small and large parish enterprises under the unified brand name 'Palanova', recently won the Kerala state award for the best FPO. Modern processing unit powering local growers Owned by over 600 farmer shareholders, the company connects nearly 10,000 farmers through partner organisations, clubs, and self-help groups. Central to SantHome's success is its state-of-the-art processing infrastructure. The facility is equipped with blanchers, pulpers, roasters, pulverisers, fruit mills, vacuum fryers, homogenisers, rice washers, steamers, ripening chambers, heat pump dryers, and advanced blast freezers. Thanks to this equipment, local farmers no longer need to rely on distant facilities to process and market their produce. The company now markets more than 50 value-added products, including frozen tapioca, frozen cut vegetables, vacuum-fried banana chips, spice blends, chutney powders, tapioca chips, and traditional snacks. According to Project Officer PV George, vacuum-fried jackfruit chips have emerged as the single most popular item in their catalogue. Global reach and strategic funding Partnering with Viswas Foods, the producer company exported 128 tonnes of processed frozen tapioca this year. Establishing the factory required an investment of 4 crore. Executive Director Fr Joseph Wattappillil explained that the unit was funded through equity from farmer shareholders, 60 lakh from the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium (SFAC), a loan of 1.17 crore from the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund, and 10 lakh from the State Horticulture Mission. The enterprise also expects an additional grant of 67 lakh under the PMFME scheme through the Department of Industries. Direct marketing and community outreach The enterprise operates a extensive nursery named Agrima along with two retail Outlets. Value-added products from member farmers and FPOs are sold through Kerala Agro Stores and Agrima Eco Shops. Through the Agrima Farmers Open Market, raw farm produce such as bananas, tubers, and eggs are sold directly to consumers, eliminating intermediaries. By 31 August, the market had procured and sold 5 tonnes of Nendran bananas, 7.5 tonnes of other banana varieties, 11 tonnes of fresh vegetables, 87,000 chicken eggs, 29,000 quail eggs, and 6.7 tonnes of exotic fruits at premium prices paid directly to growers. To help farmers secure fair prices and gain access to quality organic fertilizers, rural agricultural festivals are organised in partnership with the Karshakadalam federations. High-quality planting materials raised at the Agrima Central Nursery in Pala are also distributed at these fairs. The central nursery received financial assistance of 7.5 lakh from the Horticulture Mission...
